cues.text: Section two is digital transformation.
Let us begin with three terms that are easy to confuse.
Digitisation converts analogue information into digital form.
A good example is scanning paper invoices so that they exist as digital files.
Digitalisation goes a step further: it uses digital tools to improve existing processes.
An example is automatically approving invoices instead of having someone check each one by hand.
Digital transformation is the most far-reaching of the three.
It fundamentally changes business processes, culture, capabilities and value creation.
Think of replacing a bank that operates only through branches with an integrated digital financial platform.
People sometimes use these terms interchangeably, but the distinction is useful, so keep it in mind.
Why do organisations pursue transformation?
The drivers include changing customer expectations, competition, technological advances, regulatory pressure, efficiency requirements and new business opportunities.
But a driver alone is not enough.
Transformation requires leadership, skills, data quality, architecture, governance, and a willingness to redesign work.
Installing software alone is not transformation.
Now let us look at the main technologies, using a table.
For each one, I will give the mechanism, a business application, and a risk or limitation.
First, AI and machine learning.
The mechanism is to learn patterns from data in order to predict or generate outputs.
Business applications include fraud detection and route optimisation.
The risks are bias, inaccurate outputs, and data quality problems.
Second, blockchain.
The mechanism is a shared ledger with cryptographic integrity and consensus.
A business application is supply-chain traceability.
The risks are false inputs, governance challenges, and cost.
Third, cloud computing.
The mechanism is on-demand shared computing resources.
It supports elastic digital services.
The risks are variable bills, lock-in, and outages.
Fourth, the Internet of Things, or IoT.
The mechanism is connected sensors and devices.
Applications include fleet tracking and predictive maintenance.
The risks are device security and connectivity.
Fifth, big data analytics.
The mechanism is processing diverse, large or fast-moving datasets.
A typical application is demand forecasting.
The risks are privacy concerns and poor data quality.
Sixth, RPA, or robotic process automation.
The mechanism is automating rule-based repetitive tasks.
An application is invoice reconciliation.
The risk is brittle workflows, meaning they can break easily when something changes.
Seventh, edge computing.
The mechanism is processing data close to its source.
An application is industrial monitoring.
The risk is distributed maintenance, since many devices must be looked after.
Eighth, 5G.
The mechanism is mobile connectivity that supports high capacity and low latency in suitable deployments.
An application is connected factories.
The risks are coverage limits and infrastructure costs.
Some of these need careful qualification.
Blockchain makes recorded transactions tamper-resistant, but it does not guarantee that physical goods or initial records are authentic.
A retailer must still verify its suppliers, and verify the link between products and ledger entries.
Likewise, predictive analytics estimates future demand, but it does not eliminate uncertainty.
And cloud elasticity permits resources to expand and contract with demand, but scaling without financial controls can cause overruns.
Next, manufacturing.
Industry 4.0 integrates cyber-physical systems, sensors, automation, analytics and connected manufacturing.
Within that setting, a digital twin is a digital representation of a physical asset or process, used for monitoring and simulation.
Predictive maintenance uses telemetry to anticipate equipment failure, so that intervention can be scheduled before costly downtime occurs.
Finally, the Siemens example.
It illustrates industrial digitalisation through connected manufacturing, automation and digital twins.
The transferable lesson is to integrate technology with business processes, workforce capability and measurable outcomes, rather than copying another company's technology stack.
